Seasonal CPUE correction: impact and rebuilding saved fits

Scientific model contract v5 corrects how CPUE observations select population abundance in models with more than one season. The size of the effect depends on the data and model. The paired examples below quantify it for controlled simulations; they are not estimates of the effect on a real stock assessment.

What changed

CPUE time steps use the flattened convention

ts <- (year_index - 1L) * n_season + season_index

The old calculation used number_ysa[ts, 1, ] and selectivity from year ts. The corrected calculation decodes year_index and season_index, then uses number_ysa[year_index, season_index, ] and selectivity from that year. For example, with four seasons, ts = 4 means year 1, season 4; the old code used year 4, season 1. With one season, both calculations use exactly the same cells.

For a fixed parameter vector, this correction changes CPUE predictions and the CPUE likelihood. It does not change the underlying population trajectory or the other likelihood components. Refitting can then change parameters, population trajectories, and derived quantities. Reusing an old optimum or posterior does not account for that change.

Quantified examples

The comparison uses the complete model with 12 years, two fisheries, two CPUE indices, and multinomial length and weight compositions. It estimates log_B0 and the two log catchabilities; other parameters remain fixed. Annual catches are the same across the one-, two-, and four-season scenarios, with seasonal shares proportional to 1:n_season. A normal prior on log_B0 is centred on log(100000), with SD 0.3. CPUE and composition observations are simulated with seed 90210 under the corrected model.

Within each pair, observations, initial parameters, maps, priors, bounds, and optimiser controls are identical. Only the CPUE indexing function changes. The legacy function is frozen from main at commit 2dd8e3d (contract v4), while the rest of the model uses current code. This isolates the CPUE correction from other changes in the release. Each fit uses two nlminb() passes, with rel.tol = 1e-10, x.tol = 1e-8, and iteration/evaluation limits of 10,000.

Coverage limitation: to make both versions evaluable, the paired fits retain ts = 1:12 for each index: 24 observations in total. These span all 12 years in the single-season control, the first six years with two seasons, and the first three years with four seasons. Composition data cover all 12 years. Therefore, differences between the two- and four-season examples are not a general estimate of how bias scales with the number of seasons.

At the same starting parameters, the maximum absolute CPUE prediction changes were approximately 8.24% with two seasons and 12.28% with four seasons. Percentage changes use the legacy prediction as the denominator. The objective differences below arise entirely from CPUE.

After refitting, estimated unfished spawning output (B0) increased by approximately 4.99% and 11.71%, respectively. Terminal spawning output increased by 5.32% and 12.57%. These are conditional results from the specified simulated examples, not a universal correction factor or a bound on the possible effect. Different observation coverage, recruitment, priors, selectivity, or estimated parameter sets can give different magnitudes or signs.

All six fits returned optimiser convergence code zero, a maximum absolute gradient below 0.001, a positive-definite Hessian, and passing biological checks. In the single-season control, objectives, gradients, reports, and fitted quantities matched exactly. Existing Opakapaka golden tests separately check the bundled single-season assessment.

Full seasonal coverage can fail under the old code

The same experiment also tries observations at every seasonal time step. When ts > n_year, the old calculation attempts to select a nonexistent year from the selectivity array and raises a subscript error. The corrected models evaluate successfully. A percentage difference cannot be assigned to these failed legacy evaluations.

Which bundled assessments are affected?

The three bundled input datasets all use n_season = 1. The BET dataset has quarterly model steps represented along its n_year axis, rather than four seasons within each year. The CPUE indexing correction therefore makes no numerical change to these datasets under that convention. Calendar labels such as “quarterly” alone do not identify an affected model; inspect its dimensions and how cpue_data$ts was constructed.

The packaged opaka_quickstart_fit.rds and assessment_example.rds already record scientific contract v5. The older mcmc_fit.rds and opaka_mcmc_fit.rds are raw tmbfit objects without an Opal scientific-contract record; they cannot be certified as current from their filenames alone.

Rebuilding fits from contract v4 or earlier

Opal deliberately rejects old scientific contracts for runtime use, including single-season fits whose numerical calculations may be unchanged. Changing a version string or disabling strict checks does not rebuild or refit a model. Start from its original data, map, parameters, random-effect specification, bounds, and construction settings, then fit a new object under v5.

Before rebuilding, verify cpue_data$ts against the intended year and season. If historical inputs used year numbers instead of flattened seasonal steps, reconstruct ts from the original observation dates. Do not infer missing seasons automatically. This affects the interpretation of the data, not just the saved-file format.

The following recipe reads a legacy opal_fit or a saved opal_obj envelope for its configuration, constructs a new object, refits it, and writes a new file. It leaves the original file intact and does not copy old posterior draws or derived results. Inspect the fit diagnostics before using it.

saved <- readRDS("assessment-v4.rds")
old <- if (is.list(saved) && identical(saved$format, "opal_obj")) saved$object else saved
stopifnot(inherits(old, "opal_fit") || inherits(old, "opal_obj"))
start <- if (inherits(old, "opal_obj") && !is.null(old$fit$parameters)) {
  old$fit$parameters
} else old$parameters

# Verify old$data$cpue_data$ts before constructing the new object.
rebuilt <- opal_obj(
  data = old$data, parameters = start, map = old$map, random = old$random,
  bounds = old$bounds, control = old$control,
  makeadfun_args = old$makeadfun_args,
  metadata = list(rebuilt_from = "assessment-v4.rds")
)
rebuilt <- opal_fit(rebuilt)
rebuilt <- opal_check(rebuilt, "fit", stop_on_failure = TRUE)
opal_save(rebuilt, "assessment-v5.rds")

If posterior inference is needed, rerun opal_mcmc() against the new target, check the retained chains, and recompute residuals, summaries, and reference points. This note does not fit or certify any historical user assessment or its posterior.

The random-effect validation correction in this release is separate: it uses a numerical Hessian of the marginal objective when RTMB’s exact Hessian is unavailable. It changes diagnostic handling, not the objective or estimates. Validation records now use opal_validation_v3; rerun opal_check() when an existing v5 object’s checks show as stale. Old grid checkpoints are invalidated so the previous validation failure is not reused.

Reproduce the comparison

From the repository root, run:

Rscript --vanilla dev/seasonal-cpue/compare.R

The comparison script and frozen legacy function write the CSV evidence in inst/extdata/seasonal-cpue-impact/. Predictions at both the starting values and fitted points are retained in predictions.csv. The numerical comparison was run with the environment recorded below; it was not a fit of a real multi-season stock assessment.
